title: What If Earth's Magnetic Field Disappeared?

scenes.narration: An invisible magnetic bubble wraps around Earth. Now imagine someone flipped the switch, and it vanished.
Subscribe, then guess what goes wrong first.
That bubble deflects the solar wind, a nonstop stream of charged particles blowing off the Sun, day and night.
But here's the surprise. On the ground, you probably wouldn't feel a thing. Our thick atmosphere is the main shield, like about three meters of concrete over your head.
Earth has even had practice. The field flips roughly every million years, weakening as it does, and no mass extinction lines up with the flips.
The real danger is slow. Mars has no global magnetic field, and NASA's MAVEN probe watched the solar wind strip its air away, about a hundred grams every second.
Some travelers would lose their map, too. Young sea turtles read magnetic signatures to steer across the open ocean.
So you'd survive the day the shield switched off. But over long ages, our planet might slowly start turning into another Mars.

claims.claim: Earth's magnetosphere deflects the solar wind, a stream of charged particles from the Sun
The atmosphere, not the magnetic field, is the main shield against energetic particles, equivalent to about 10 feet (3 m) of concrete
Magnetic reversals happen about every million years or so and no mass extinctions correlate with them
During a reversal the magnetic field weakens but does not completely disappear
Mars lacks a global magnetic field; MAVEN measured the solar wind stripping its upper atmosphere at roughly 100 grams (a quarter pound) per second
Young sea turtles use regional magnetic fields as open-ocean navigational markers
Over long times, losing the field could let the solar wind erode Earth's upper atmosphere as on Mars (speculative, phrased with 'might')
